title: Becoming Boston: Eight Moments in the Geography of a Changing City
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Note: This exhibition is held in the Leventhal Map and Education Gallery which is open Tuesday 11am-5pm, Wednesday 1pm-7pm, Thursday - Saturday 11am - 5pm, Sunday 1pm - 5pm. Please check their website for the most up to date hours and schedule.Maps trace out the complicated history of places, and we can use them to document geography in much the same way that we can use diaries and letters to document biography. In the eight cases of this exhibition, we follow the changing spatial forms of the place we now call Boston—from before the landscape carried that name all the way through the struggles, clashes, and dreams that continue to reshape the city today. These maps don’t merely depict facts about how the city looked at different moments in its history. Instead, they invite us to contemplate how geographic forces, both natural and human, have constructed the physical and social world around us, through large and small transformations that have transpired over many centuries. The Leventhal Map & Education Center regularly mounts exhibitions in our gallery, located in the historic McKim Building in the Boston Public Library in Copley Square. All of our exhibitions feature scholarly research as well as activities for families, children, and educators. Our permanent exhibit, Becoming Boston: Eight Moments in the Geography of a Changing City, is available any time our public gallery is open. Visit the digital exhibition to Becoming Boston here. title: Declarations: Printing a New Nation
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Note: This exhibition is held in the Leventhal Map and Education Gallery which is open Tuesday 11am-5pm, Wednesday 1pm-7pm, Thursday - Saturday 11am - 5pm, Sunday 1pm - 5pm. Please check their website for the most up to date hours and schedule. On July 4, 1776, the Continental Congress ratified the Declaration of Independence in Philadelphia. The next day, the first printed copies were sent off and began to circulate throughout the thirteen colonies, which were now, on paper, independent states. Throughout July and August of 1776, the Declaration was reprinted in major American cities and small towns alike. Some of these new printings appeared in newspapers. Others were issued as large, single-sheet publications known as broadsides. Many versions, in both formats, were printed before the delegates to the Continental Congress began to sign the official handwritten Declaration in early August. These early printings of the Declaration were created at a time when the independence of the future United States was anything but certain. From the perspective of those who read it in the summer of 1776, we can see the Declaration of Independence in its original form: not yet a famous founding document, but breaking news. In the exhibition Declarations: Printing a New Nation, see eight different original printings of the Declaration of Independence, and take a journey that explores how the news of independence spread out from Philadelphia in the summer of 1776 when the ink was not yet dry on the founding documents of a new nation. title: Lexicon
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] July 2026Aluminum · 18 × 18 × 2 ftAlfonso Parra Rubio · Erik StrandMIT Center for Bits and Atoms Lexicon is a free-form structural shell built from individual origami-folded cells assembled into a two-sided lattice, or interlocking framework. The folding and assembling process creates a structure that is as strong and rigid as typical building methods, but it is much lighter. The structure is made for this space, Deferrari Hall. Its light, curved shape contrasts with the Boylston Street Building's heavy and blocky brutalist architecture. Lexicon's three pointed shape is a reference to Rafael Guastavino's tiled ceilings in the Central Library's McKim Building. By bringing together influences from both of the Central Library's buildings, Lexicon celebrates the role of geometry in design and construction. A collaboration between the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), the Boston Public Library (BPL), and the Mayor's Office of Arts and Culture (MOAC). With Riccardo Foschi (University of Bologna), Rupert Malec (University of Innsbruck), Tomohiro Tachi (University of Tokyo), and Neil Gershenfeld (MIT Center for Bits and Atoms). Made possible and funded by MOAC.

About the book: From one of the world’s most celebrated intellectuals, a “fascinating” (Financial Times), brilliantly insightful work that explains how we think about each other’s thoughts about each other’s thoughts, ad infinitum. It sounds impossible, but “superlatively gifted science writer” (The Times) Steven Pinker shows that we do it all the time. This awareness, which we experience as something that is public or “out there,” is called common knowledge, and it has a momentous impact on our social, political, and economic lives. Author bio: Steven Pinker is the Johnstone Professor of Psychology at Harvard University. He has won many prizes for his teaching, his research on language, cognition, and social relations, and his twelve books, including The Language Instinct, How the Mind Works, The Better Angels of Our Nature, and Rationality. He is an elected member of the National Academy of Sciences, a two-time Pulitzer Prize finalist, and one of Time’s “100 Most Influential People in the World Today.” Talks for Better Living The City-Wide Friends of the Boston Public Library and the Boston Public Library invite you to a series of talks featuring world class authors. title: Everyone Wants a Long Life. Nobody Wants to Get Old.
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Join us for this afternoon in-person talk in partnership with the Boston Village. Advances in medicine and public health have culminated in people rightly expecting to have a long life. And yet, we almost universally don't want to "get old." Here in the US, being "old" is associated with decline in function, abilities, connection, independence and, ultimately, with loss of relevance and worth. Join us as Marie Clouqueur guides us to the possibility of maintaining our value and dignity in older age, even with limitations and loss. Drawing on her clinical work in geriatric psychiatry as well as examples in history and literature, Clouqueur will invite us to see older adults as protagonists who can drive the next advancements of our society. About the speaker: Marie Clouqueur, LICSW, is a clinical social worker at McLean Hospital specializing in older adults and family work. She founded and leads the dementia support program in the Division of Geriatric Psychiatry. Her clinical work provides group and individual psychotherapy to improve caregiver resilience and to support people living with dementia. Marie Clouqueur is speaking as a part of Boston Village's 25th Anniversary Speaker Series titled Aging in Place: Living Your Best Life @ Home. title: Exhibition: Life, Liberty, and the Pursuit of Happiness
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] To mark the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence, the Boston Public Library's Community History Department partnered with Revolutionary Spaces to offer a free and public program series called "Life, Liberty, and the Pursuit of Happiness." Named for the unalienable rights identified in the Declaration—rights that inherently belong to all human beings, and that governments are created to protect—these programs brought people together to explore, question, and find inspiration in the Declaration of Independence. During two printmaking workshops and four declaration writing workshops at the BPL, library visitors reflected on the 250th anniversary of the American Revolution. Displayed together, the art prints and writing pieces made by community members speak to the ongoing American struggle to create and sustain a free society. As a viewer of the exhibition, we invite you to consider: How do I identify with this nation's founding document? What do I celebrate? How do I use my voice in protest? About Community History The BPL Community History Department aims to democratize the expression of history by supporting people in their efforts to document the stories of themselves and their communities. We offer resources, programs, and support for local and community history work based on people’s lived experiences, knowledge, and expertise. About Revolutionary Spaces Revolutionary Spaces stewards the historic Old South Meeting House and Old State House as landmarks, museums, and active civic spaces. Its mission is to bring people together to explore the American struggle to create and sustain a free society—using history as a powerful tool for civic engagement and public dialogue. For more information, visit RevolutionarySpaces.org or follow them on social media at @RevSpaces. Accessibility Notice: We strive to make our events accessible. title: Author Talk: Emily Sweeney - Dropkick Murphy : A Legendary Life
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Join Boston Globe reporter Emily Sweeney with her authentic Boston accent, for a discussion of her biography of local luminary Dr. John Murphy, aka "Dropkick" Murphy and his life in and outside the wrestling arena. Newspapers called him the “the man with the cast-iron toes,” “the best drop-kicker in wrestling,” and “one of the mat game’s biggest box office attractions.” But Dr. John “Dropkick” Murphy’s legacy extends far beyond the wrestling ring. Decades before the Betty Ford Center became a household name — and long before the band the Dropkick Murphys named themselves in his honor — the phrase going to Dropkick’s meant a person struggling with addiction needed help and would soon get some. This book chronicles for the first time the unbelievable life of Dr. “Dropkick” Murphy, a professional wrestler who put himself through medical school during the Great Depression and then opened Bellows Farm in Acton, MA, a one-of-a-kind institution that served as both a facility where elite athletes could train as well as a secluded place where down-on-their-luck alcoholics could go to sober up discreetly. The celebrities who frequented Dropkick Murphy’s farm were many, and numerous professional athletes would go there to focus on their training and work out in his state-of-the-art gymnasium. As a result, Bellows Farm featured an unrivaled and revolving cast of colorful characters who brought it to life. Drawing on years of research and interviews, author Emily Sweeney goes behind the scenes to reveal the untold story of Murphy’s life, his farm, and the legendary events that unfolded there. Emily Sweeney is a staff reporter at the Boston Globe and author of the books Boston Organized Crime and Gangland Boston. A proud native of Dorchester, she also appears in Bloody Boston, a two-part documentary special on the Reelz channel; Stranger Than Fiction: The True Story of Whitey Bulger, Southie, and The Departed, a bonus feature on the DVD of the Oscar-winning movie The Departed; and the forthcoming Netflix series How To Become A Mob Boss. description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Join us for a screening of the feature-length documentary Papertown as a part of the 2026 Boston Film Festival. description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Join us in person or over Zoom Webinar as the Boston Public Library welcomes Sarah Botstein as a speaker for the Lowell Lecture Series. As a filmmaker who has worked closely with Ken Burns for over 30 years as a part of Florentine Films, Sarah will talk about her latest film, PBS's The American Revolution, historical filmmaking, and the revolutionary techniques that Florentine Films uses to bring history to life. Botstein will be in conversation with Imari Paris Jeffries from Embrace Boston and the program will be introduced by BPL President David Leonard. After the main program, in-person audience members can meet the speaker in the Connector Space located just outside of Rabb Hall. This program will happen in-person and over Zoom Webinar. We plan to open doors twenty minutes in advance for our in-person audience. Sarah Botstein has worked with Ken Burns for nearly 30 years and produced some of his most popular and acclaimed documentaries on PBS. Most recently, she produced and co-directed The American Revolution. Her previous work includes The U.S. and the Holocaust, Hemingway, College Behind Bars, The Vietnam War, Prohibition, The War, and Jazz. Botstein also works closely with PBS LearningMedia to develop educational materials as part of the Ken Burns Classroom, and she was an original contributor to Ken Burns's UNUM. Botstein is now working on a three-part series about Lyndon B. Johnson and the Great Society. Sarah Botstein is joined by Imari Paris Jeffries, CEO of Embrace Boston. Imari Paris Jeffries , Ph.D., is President and CEO of Embrace, an arts, culture, and community organization reshaping public memory as public policy and advancing belonging through justice. His work begins with a simple premise: cities are shaped not only by policy and economics, but by story, monument, silence, and who is remembered. Under his leadership, Embrace has grown into a civic force committed to centering Black life in public space. The Embrace Monument on Boston Common honoring Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. and Coretta Scott King stands as a declaration that love, struggle, and Black life belong at the heart of the city's landscape. What began as a monument has evolved into a movement, paired with institutional commitments designed to shift culture in lasting ways. Beyond this first monument, Imari has advanced collaboration on the WEB Du Bois Monument and a forthcoming national arts and civic center in Downtown Crossing, envisioned as a twenty-first century civic home where culture and democracy meet. Before leading Embrace, Imari served in executive leadership roles at Parenting Journey, the Italian Home for Children, Jumpstart, Boston Rising, and Friends of the Children Boston, consistently strengthening governance, stabilizing finances, and embedding equity as an operational discipline. A dedicated civic leader, Imari serves as a Trustee of the University of Massachusetts System and on the boards of Boston Ballet and GBH. He has been recognized among Boston Magazine's 100 Most Influential Bostonians and is a recipient of the Mel King Social Innovator Award. A four-time graduate of UMass Boston, and a United States Army veteran, he lives in Boston with his family This program is produced in partnership with GBH and PBS. title: Author Talk: N.K. Jemisin on Revolutionary Ideas in Fantasy Fiction
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] In-person registration is full with a waitlist. Please register to attend virtually HERE.Noted and award-winning fantasy fiction author N.K. Jemisin discusses her work and her 20-plus-year career that has been inspired by revolutionary ideas. N. K. Jemisin is a fantasy author and 2020 MacArthur Fellow. Since beginning her professional career in the early 2000s, her short fiction and novels have been recognized with multiple Hugo, Nebula, and Locus Awards. Most of her works have been optioned for television or film, and collectively her novels, including the Broken Earth trilogy, have sold over two million copies. After twenty years working in higher education as an applied counseling psychologist, she “retired” in 2016 to become a full-time writer, writing instructor, and public speaker. Her speculative works range widely in theme, though with repeated motifs: resistance and oppression, loneliness and belonging, and Wouldn’t It Be Cool If This One Ridiculous Thing Happened. In her spare time she’s into tabletop and video games, biking, fanfiction, and urban gardening. She lives in Brooklyn with her son and two cats. After the talk, N.K. Jemisin will sign copies of her books with our local bookstore partner, Trident Booksellers. Accessibility Notice: We strive to make our events accessible. title: 2026 Maury A. Bromsen Humanistic Literary Arts Lecture: Ann Patchett (Full—registration and the waitlist are closed)
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] In-person AND online registration seats are full. Registration and the waitlist are closed. Author Ann Patchett headlines the 2026 Maury A. Bromsen Lecture. Ann Patchett has been the recipient of numerous awards, including a National Humanities Medal and the PEN/Faulkner Award. Her novel, The Dutch House, was a finalist for the Pulitzer Prize. She was named one of TIME’s 100 Most Influential People in the World and is a member of the American Academy of Arts and Letters. Her books have been both New York Times Notable Books and New York Times bestsellers, and her work has been translated into more than thirty languages. The Maury A. Bromsen Lecture Series at the Boston Public Library was established to celebrate authors whose work illuminates the depth, dignity, and complexity of the human experience. In its renewed form, the series will foreground literature that brings individual lives fully into view—work that reflects Maury Bromsen’s vision of humanistic bibliography by exploring how personal narratives, lived experience, and moral imagination shape our collective understanding of history, culture, and community. The lecture offers a space for distinguished writers to reflect on their creative journeys, share insights into their recent work, and consider how storytelling can deepen empathy and understanding in a complex world. description: [Central Library in Copley Square] We are a book group for adults that reads a wide variety of fiction and nonfiction. We meet the 3rd* Wednesday of every month at 2:30 p.m. at the Central Library in Copley Square and on Zoom. Our choice for October is The Anxious Generation by Jonathan Haidt. Nonfiction. Social psychologist Jonathan Haidt lays out the facts about the epidemic of teen mental illness that hit many countries at the same time. title: Lowell Lecture: AI and Civic Engagement with Nathan Sanders, Dr. Avijit Ghosh, Jessica Chapel and David Leonard
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Join us in person or over Zoom Webinar as the Boston Public Library welcomes AI experts Nathan Sanders, Dr. Avijit Ghosh, and Jessica Chapel as panelists for this conversation about AI and civic engagement as a part of the 2026 Lowell Lecture Series. This program will be moderated by BPL President David Leonard. Jessica Chapel is Chief of Digital & Online Services at Boston Public Library, where she leads digitization, digital stewardship, and UX, with a growing focus on AI's role in information access and discovery. Her department operates Digital Commonwealth, the statewide repository connecting 270+ Massachusetts libraries, archives, and museums. She co-hosts an ongoing speaker series with the Leventhal Map & Education Center on AI and cultural heritage collections, and co-moderates BPL's AI Interest Group. Dr. Avijit Ghosh is a Lead Technical AI Policy Researcher at Hugging Face 🤗, a central platform for open AI models, datasets, and research tools used by industry, government, and academic developers worldwide. He is also a Research Affiliate at the University of Connecticut. His work sits at the intersection of AI research and policy, with a central focus on how we measure and benchmark AI systems, and whether those measurements can actually be trusted. He founded and leads the EvalEval Coalition, a multi-stakeholder initiative bringing methodological rigor and accountability to AI evaluation. His broader research spans algorithmic bias, agent autonomy, AI for science, and third-party flaw disclosure, with coverage in The New York Times, Forbes, The Guardian, ProPublica, Wired, and MIT Technology Review. He represents Hugging Face in technical engagements with legislators and regulators in the United States, United Kingdom, European Union, and Singapore on open-source AI governance and evaluation standards. His work has helped shape AI regulation in New York City and prompted Facebook to remove its biased ad targeting algorithm. Nathan E. Sanders is a data scientist focused on making policymaking more participatory. His research spans machine learning, astrophysics, public health, environmental justice, and more. He has served in fellowships and the Massachusetts legislature and the Berkman-Klein Center at Harvard University. You can find his writing on AI and democracy in publications like The New York Times and The Atlantic and at his website, nsanders.me. After the main program, in-person audience members can meet the speakers in the Connector Space located just outside of Rabb Hall. This program will happen in-person and over Zoom Webinar. We plan to open doors twenty minutes in advance for our in-person audience. Please note: registration will open six weeks before the program date, on Wednesday September 9 at 6:00 pm. title: Author Talk: Courtney Humphries - Climate Change and the Future of Boston
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Join us as author Courtney Humphries discusses her new book on the climate impacts facing Boston and the city’s efforts to mitigate and adapt to a changing climate.Like many of the world’s iconic coastal cities, Boston faces potentially severe impacts from climate change. Depending on global emissions, Boston could face several feet of sea level rise this century, which would leave many parts of the city subject to tidal and storm flooding. Precipitation events could become more frequent and extreme, and its already-humid summers could become dangerously hot, with most days over 90 degrees. Today, Boston is a booming city with a growing population, a glittering new waterfront neighborhood, world-class universities and a strong economy. Its future risks and opportunities related to climate change are shaped by the 400-year environmental, social and economic history of the city’s development. Climate Change and the Future of Boston describes how Boston’s history and current context shape future climate impacts and examines the mitigation and adaptation strategies the city has taken. Boston is a leader in acknowledging the problem of climate change; it has set a goal of becoming carbon neutral by 2050, among other climate-related goals. It has also developed science-based climate models and undertaken a robust planning process to identify strategies to protect its waterfront from flooding and increase its resilience to other climate-related impacts. Its mayor has embraced a progressive Green New Deal for Boston emphasizing the need for an inclusive and equitable approach to climate mitigation and adaptation. But the city also faces structural challenges, such as aging infrastructure, historic racial inequities, rising gentrification and income inequality and ongoing political and regulatory obstacles that hinder efforts to adapt in an efficient and just manner. She will conclude with a set of forward-looking scenarios about what the future may have in store for the city and the lessons it holds for other coastal cities struggling with these challenges.Courtney Humphries, PhD, is an interdisciplinary scholar, teacher, and award-winning journalist writing about science and the urban environment. title: Author Talk with Peggy Levitt—Move Over, Mona Lisa
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Join us for an author talk and signing with Peggy Levitt, Wellesley College professor and renowned sociologist. In her new book, Move Over, Mona Lisa, Peggy asks: If the public is loudly calling for a wider range of art, literature, and ideas in our museums, libraries, and classrooms, why are our cultural and educational institutions so slow in making the change? Her answer is what she calls the "inequality pipeline," the layers of obstacles that keep art and ideas from circulating freely across the globe. Drawing on conversations with artists, writers, and cultural professionals in Argentina, Lebanon, and South Korea, Peggy shows that many of them have stopped waiting for old gatekeepers to change and are instead building new, alternative hubs and pathways that let art and ideas travel from cities like "Buenos Aires to Mexico City without having to pass through Madrid." Peggy takes us from the studios and desks where art and ideas are first created, through the museums and institutions that circulate and exhibit them, to the classrooms where they're researched and taught. Along the way, she reveals how cities, museums, and libraries influence more about both what creatives do and what the public learns than we might generally assume. The result is a hopeful, sharply observed new theory of how global cultural and intellectual change really happens. Peggy Levitt is the Mildred Lane Kemper Chair of Sociology at Wellesley College. She is also a co-founder of the Global (De)Centre. Her latest book, Move Over, Mona Lisa: Reimagining What We Read, Look At, and Learn was published this year by Stanford University Press. Peggy has previously written on social protections across borders, museums as site of immigration and national story-building, the influence of immigration on religion, and the socio-political realities of 1st and 2nd generation American immigrants. She co-directed the Transnational Studies Initiative and the Politics and Social Change Workshop at the Weatherhead Center for International Affairs at Harvard University and the Hauser Center for Nonprofit Organizations at the Harvard Kennedy School from 1998 to 2020. Peggy received Honorary Doctoral Degrees from the University of Helsinki (2017) and from Maastricht University (2014) and has held numerous fellowships and guest professorships at academic and research institutions from Edinburgh to Hong Kong.Accessibility Notice: We strive to make our events accessible. description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Patrons and visitors are invited to handwrite the U.S. Constitution in Bates Hall at the Central Library in Copley Square. This art practice was created so that people will know their rights, deepen their understanding of laws created to protect these rights, and to help resist negative thinking. The goal of this art practice is to encourage people to hold their own Handwriting sessions on a recurring basis; to create a physical and psychological space that explores the practice of concentrated writing as an art form, and a process designed to bring people together in a quiet and calming way, all by focusing on human rights. It has been identified as a powerful and transformative form of activism for introverts. Accessibility Notice: We strive to make our events accessible. title: Author Talk: Linford D. Fisher — Stealing America: The Hidden Story of Indigenous Slavery in U.S. History
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Join author Linford Fisher in a discussion of his book, Stealing America, where he shows that although the first enslaved Africans arrived in Jamestown in 1619, European slavery in America began more than a century before. The enslavement of Indigenous people began in the years just after 1492, ensnaring an estimated three to six million Natives throughout the Americas. Although largely erased from the public consciousness, Native enslavement continued for centuries to become a colossal phenomenon that affected nearly 600,000 Native Americans in North America alone, revealing the shocking truth that American colonizers enslaved Natives in roughly the same numbers as they imported enslaved Africans. From Virginia to California, from New England to Barbados, Stealing America traces the history of Indigenous enslavement and land dispossession, detailing how colonizers captured Natives and often deliberately mislabeled them as Black slaves to avoid detection. While the American Revolution pealed the bells of freedom for colonists, it paved a larcenous trail of westward expansion that subsequently plundered Indigenous land and stole the labor of Natives from nations like the Cherokee, Navajo, Nisean, and many others. “This double theft,” Fisher writes, “was central to the origins, growth, and eventual success of the English colonies and the United States—not just initially but throughout all of American history.” Fisher will weave together accounts of major episodes in American history including early colonization, the American Revolution, and the Civil War with lesser-known stories of Native enslavement and land loss. Fisher upends conventional histories about the nature of American slavery, revealing enslaved Natives in places we have overlooked, including southern antebellum plantations and the nineteenth-century American West. After Congress outlawed Native slavery in 1867, Americans forced Indigenous children into boarding schools and white homes, where they labored under forced assimilation. This practice was not reformed until the latter twentieth century, when Native nations finally secured increasing rights and self-determination. Linford D. Fisher is an associate professor of history at Brown University. The author of The Indian Great Awakening and principal investigator of the Stolen Relations project, he lives in Providence, Rhode Island. title: Author Talk: Paul Lewis — An Embattled Poet, a Pilloried Bird: How Poe's "Raven" Became America's Most Famous Poem
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Join Boston College Professor Emeritus Paul Lewis in a discussion of his new book on Edgar Allan Poe's famous poem. In 1845, over 5,300 poems were published in American magazines. Most immediately began their deserved descent into oblivion. Poe's "Raven" stands as the most conspicuous exception to this. But why? What factors influenced the attention devoted to "The Raven" from the day when it was first published? Why was it widely reprinted, praised, criticized, and mocked during the next weeks and months? Why did it inspire parodies that replaced Poe's "saintly bird of yore" with a veritable menagerie of other animals—including an owl, gazelle, turkey, pig, dog, cats, rats, and (eek!) bedbugs? And how did Poe's reputation—as a literary brawler and harsh book reviewer and as a man who struggled with money and alcohol—play into the reception of "The Raven"? Signed copies of Paul Lewis' Quothing "The Raven" The First Responses to America's Most Famous Poem will be available at this book-launch event. Paul Lewis is a Professor Emeritus at Boston College, a past president of the Poe Studies Association, and the curator of exhibitions on literary Boston. As the Board of Directors chair of the Edgar Allan Poe Foundation of Boston, Inc., Lewis worked with others to celebrate Poe in the city of his birth by having a square at the intersection of Boylston Street and Charles Street South dedicated to Poe in 2010 and then installing a statue of Poe in it in 2014. title: Handwriting the Constitution
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Patrons and visitors are invited to handwrite the U.S. Constitution in Bates Hall at the Central Library in Copley Square. This program aims to create time and a quiet space to reflect and deepen one's understanding of this historic document. All supplies will be provided. Participants will first stop by the supply table outside of Bates Hall to pick up writing supplies and a copy of the Constitution, before proceeding to Bates Hall. Reproductions of John Adams's personal copy of the Constitution held by Special Collections will also be available to transcribe. This program is self-paced. Patrons are invited to stay for the whole session or simply stay as long as they would like. About Handwriting the Constitution Handwriting the Constitution is a social art project begun in 2017 by artist Morgan O'Hara. It invites people from all walks of life to meet in public spaces to handwrite the U.S. Constitution or other documents written to protect human rights and freedoms. This art practice was created so that people will know their rights, deepen their understanding of laws created to protect these rights, and to help resist negative thinking. The goal of this art practice is to encourage people to hold their own Handwriting sessions on a recurring basis; to create a physical and psychological space that explores the practice of concentrated writing as an art form, and a process designed to bring people together in a quiet and calming way, all by focusing on human rights. It has been identified as a powerful and transformative form of activism for introverts. Accessibility Notice: We strive to make our events accessible.
